title: The blind prince
hookLine: a frightened widow shuts her eyes, a prince is born blind, and the Gita's first voice arrives
tomorrow: a second widow, and a maid who knows how to welcome a guest.
last: SHE THINKS OF HIM. HE COMES.

cards: Vyasa comes to the palace straight from the forest, and he looks it. The text describes him: dark skin, matted hair the color of copper, a rough beard, blazing eyes, and a smell no one would call perfume.
His mother has asked him to give the house of the Kurus a son. He agrees, and asks that they wait first. Satyavati answers: there is no time.

teach.h: AN OLD CUSTOM FOR A LINE.
teach.b: This starts a new part: the fathers of the cousins. In those days, when a king died without sons, a learned man could be asked to father an heir in his name. Vyasa asks that the widows first keep a vow.
Satyavati says the kingdom can't wait. So the elder widow, Ambika, is told someone will come tonight.
The lamp is lit, in walks the sage with blazing eyes and copper hair, and she's so afraid she shuts her eyes and keeps them shut.
Afterward Vyasa tells his mother: the son will be strong and wise, but because his mother closed her eyes, he'll be born blind. That son is Dhritarashtra. Here's why Hindus still know his name.

Years later, the Bhagavad Gita, one of Hinduism's most loved books, opens with this blind king. He asks what happened on the battlefield, and he says: my sons, and the sons of Pandu. Many teachers stop right there.
Mine, and theirs. They read his blindness two ways: his eyes, and his heart.

Hindus have a word for that second blindness: moha, attachment so strong it stops you seeing clearly. It's one of six inner enemies the tradition names. And near its end, the Gita has Arjuna say his moha is gone.
The whole book walks from a blind 'mine' to clear sight. Today it looks like a parent who can't see what their own kid did, or a fan who can't see their team's foul. Love isn't the problem.
Love that can only say 'mine' is.

how: The ancient custom in this story, called niyoga, is described in old texts and the epics; it is not practiced in Hindu families today. Many Hindus who read the Gita hear its first verse, Dhritarashtra's question about 'my sons', as the start of its teaching on moha.

s: Dhritarashtra's blindness only matters for the throne
many teachers read it as a picture of moha too: a father who can't see past 'mine'.
the Bhagavad Gita opens with Dhritarashtra's question
he asks what his sons and Pandu's sons did at Kurukshetra.
moha is the confusion of attachment, one of six inner enemies the tradition names.

games.q: your little cousin shoves a kid at a party. his parents say 'he'd never do that.' by Dhritarashtra's story, what's going on?
o: moha: love for 'mine' is blocking their sight.
they're right; family always comes first.
they're lying on purpose to protect him.
games.why: the tradition's word is moha. not wickedness: a love that can only see 'mine'. the Gita starts there, and ends with Arjuna's moha gone.

practice: Bring to mind someone you call yours: a child, a sibling, a friend, a team. Picture them clearly, the good and the not-so-good, the way an honest neighbor would see them. If you pray, hold them before God and ask to see them truly.
If you don't, just let your eyes stay open to all of them. Love doesn't need you to look away.

wordCard.voice: Dhritarashtra, born blind because his frightened mother shut her eyes, and the first voice you hear in the Bhagavad Gita.

orig.note: Sanskrit Dhritarashtra: Ambika's son, born blind, the elder of the cousins' fathers.

carryVoice: Your line: moha, the blindness of 'mine'. A blind king's first question, and a whole book to answer it. See you tomorrow.
